text:
Stay right of the gully that divides the two spires, and scramble to a flat ledge. Those are the two things to find: the dividing gully, kept on your left, and a flat ledge where the route starts.

Why the gully is the right handrail to use here: North and South Early Winters Spires are separated by a single continuous cleft, a chockstone-filled chasm on the west side and a gully on the east. It runs the full height between the two peaks, so it is the one feature on this side you cannot lose. Keep it on your left and you are on North Early Winters Spire's ground; cross it and you are on South Early Winters Spire, where the Direct East Buttress and Southern Man start.

Arrival: a flat ledge, gained by scrambling. Flat ground on a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation.

The trailhead test, which is the one that costs an hour if you get it wrong: this route is on the east side and is reached from the hairpin pullout. The other two North Early Winters Spire routes here, The West Face and Labor Pains, are on the west side and are reached from the Blue Lake Trailhead, which is about 2.5 miles away by road on the far side of Washington Pass. Those are different cars.

And the descent crosses back over the mountain, which you should plan for before starting: from the summit, traverse to the west side of the peak and rappel either the Chockstone Route with a 60 m rope or the bolted West Face anchors with a 70 m rope. Both require crossing over from the east-side climbing line to the west-side descent infrastructure.

edits.new: Keep to the right of the gully splitting the pair of spires, and scramble up onto a flat ledge.

text: The only ridge in the area with large trees on it, then a cliffy nuisance ridge. Cross Glacier Creek above the falls and traverse nearly level to the base of a timbered ridge — unmistakable, because it is the only rib on this slope carrying big trees while everything either side of it is brush and talus. That ridge is the first landmark and it is climbed, not skirted. The second comes at the end of the upper traverse near 5,100 ft: a cliffy ridge that has to be got around rather than crossed. Once past it, turn right and go straight up the talus slopes toward the summit gully. At the gully entrance the season decides the day — in a good year the snowfield runs continuously into the gully, and where it has pulled back, the rock immediately to its left has gone at short class 4. The gully above is mostly class 3 and finishes at a notch on the skyline just west of the true summit; aim for that notch, not for the summit block. A gully topping out at the summit, or east of it, is the wrong one.

text: The East Ridge is not reversed as a rappel line in its own right; two descents are used instead. The standard one is the East Ledges, dropping climber's-right/northeast directly off the summit: three rappels trend northeast from the summit area, then a short, exposed grassy traverse east to the next rock rib, followed by two more rappels onto the East Ledges proper, about 5 rappels in all. From there, several hundred metres of loose, sandy and grassy class 3–4 ledges and slabs, marked by intermittent and sometimes doubled cairn lines, lead east above the cliffs over the crevassed Boston Glacier to a gully about 100 ft below the Solitary Gendarme; go up and over the East Ridge through it, then down snow slopes on the south side to the small glacier below Forbidden's south face and the walk back across Boston Basin. The alternative is to reverse along the ridge crest past the gendarmes to the West Ridge notch and descend the West Ridge line: about three rappels on the ridge and about five down the Cat Scratch gullies, roughly eight on a single 60 m rope. It is longer, but it is more travelled and easier to follow, and many parties prefer it to the East Ledges, which are faster but loose, exposed, rockfall-prone and easy to lose. Either way, expect mostly natural slung-horn and block anchors with some tat and a handful of fixed or bolted stations, and carry a 60 m rope.

text: Forbidden's tallest, steepest, and most remote established route, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Ed Cooper in July 1959. text: From the Boston Basin trailhead off Cascade River Road, follow the unsigned but well-beaten Boston Basin climbers' path. It starts by following the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about 1 mile, then splits off the roadbed to climb steeply and directly through forest. The trail crosses four seasonal creeks/streams (reliable water) as it switchbacks up through increasingly open timber, breaking out above treeline around 5,300 ft. Above treeline it continues into the broad boulder-and-heather Boston Basin cirque, past the usual high-camp sites around 6,300–6,600 ft (roughly 4–5 miles and 3–4 hours from the car, ringed by Sahale, Sharkfin Tower, and Mt. Torment). From camp, make an ascending traverse across talus and the Quien Sabe Glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face; when the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often a faster, drier alternative to crossing snow/ice. Rope up if the glacier is crevassed or snow-covered. Aim for the obvious ~500-ft snow-and-ice couloir splitting the left edge of the south face — the standard gully leading to the West Ridge notch. This couloir steepens to 40–50°+ near its top, typically wants crampons/axe (and sometimes a picket) into mid-summer, and is guarded by a moat near its top, against the rock walls approaching the notch, that can require a short steep step or a band of loose rock to surmount. Exiting the couloir at the ridge-crest notch is roughly 4–5 hours and about 4,500 ft above the trailhead.

text: Stay west of the stream, and do not climb the gully it comes out of. Three gullies drain this face and they are not equivalent. The eastern one is where the stream originates, and it is the one that can cliff-band you out — which is exactly why every description of this route tells you to stay west of the stream from the meadows upward. The central open gully and slopes just west of the stream is the most direct line and tops out at the saddle southeast of the summit. A further large gully west of that reaches the saddle southwest of the true summit, between the mountain's two highpoints. The transition to watch for is at about 7,100 ft where meadow turns to rock and the scree begins; above it you climb directly up steep rocky slopes, picking over scree and rock buttresses. At the top the ground flattens onto a high plateau and the summit sits on the ridge crest, wide and gentle. If you are standing on a pointed bump with higher ground to the north, you are on one of the sub-peaks southeast of the true top.

edits.new: Farther west, a second large gully reaches the saddle between the mountain's two highpoints, southwest of the true summit.

text: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.

text: Descend the line of ascent. A single 70 m rope handles it (60 m would probably work) via five or more rappels off trees and horns, linked by long stretches of downscrambling in the gully. Rappelling off the overhang near the summit into Gully #2 has been done, but getting out to that rappel is described as quite scary and it is not recommended. Below the Y Notch you are back on the Main Peak's South Route descent — a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, then the slab (two double-rope rappels if you rope it) and the dirt gully. Loose rock is the constant theme; the descent is where parties get hurt.

text: The old sketch landmarks are still the way people navigate it: dirt gully, slab, canyon edge, tiny notch, razorback, glade saddle, key ledge traverse, Y notch, #2 gully. Walk up the dry creek bed from the road; partway up the route leaves the streambed into the woods on faint trail and flagging. At about 2,200 ft you reach the dirt gully — fill water at the creek here, it is the last certain water on the route. Four hundred vertical feet of loose dirt and rock, then the trail exits left into brush-free timber for another 400 ft, then the slab, which is two pitches of comfortable soloing on intersecting dikes. Above the slab continue in dirt along its upper left edge, traverse under a rock outcrop, over the razorback and tiny notch to the Glade Saddle, where there is a tight, well-used two-person bivy site. The wooded ramp above has a sporty 20-foot step. The Key Ledge Traverse is the most overstated part of the description — after the dirt gully it feels like a walk. It ends at the Y Notch, the confluence of #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon. A short exposed step around a rock band, then several hundred yards of very steep brush and brush-tunnel on faint trail, brings you to the base of #2 Gully. The gully is a nightmarish mix of impossibly loose rock on one side and polished mossy rock on the other — do not attempt it unless bone dry. Simulclimb the lower section with short belayed steps, then pitch out the harder ground; a fixed ring piton partway up may date to the 1940 first ascent. The 'Chimney Variation' (two leads of easy class 5 above the chimney, a good idea if the chimney is wet) rejoins the standard line at the top of #2 Gully around 5,200 ft, from where easy slabs and steep heather lead to the summit.

text: From the summit scramble down to the top of the easy slab and rig a single-rope rappel to the col at the top of #2 Gully. From there scramble to a bolted rappel station and make the first of about four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes, traversing 100-yard stretches of slab between stations on the east side of the gully; the lower stations are on trees and chockstones with slings dating back to the 1990s. Pack the ropes near the base of the gully and downclimb — this is where the west-side rock is loosest and where a party member was struck by a 500-pound block that cut loose under hand pressure in 2001. Cross back over the Y Notch and the Key Ledge Traverse, make a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, and continue down past the Glade Saddle. Two more double-rope rappels land you at the base of the slab at 2,900 ft; from there it is the wooded ridge, then the dirt gully to the creek at 2,100 ft, then the faint trail and the dry creek bed to the car. Expect to lose the trail in the dark at least once.

text: Gato Negro is a full-day alpine rock climb with fairly sustained 5.10a/b climbing spread across 12 long pitches. Most pitches span 180-190 feet with none shorter than 150 feet. The route features a spectacular hand-crack first pitch, bolted 5.10a face climbing on fragile flakes, rising traverses under roofs, and splitter cracks on the final headwall. Route-finding is somewhat challenging; avoid a clean blocky chimney to the right of the route that looks good but is not as good as it appears. Cruxes are mostly well-protected, but a few slightly runout 5.8 sections on loose granite and a 5.9+ offwidth chimney section present additional challenges.

text: The descent does not reverse the route. Make a few rappels over the top of the spire into the steep gully between Whine Spire and the west summit of Silver Star, then work down the gully with long sections of loose 4th-class downclimbing and a few more rappels. The gully is extremely loose, with rock coming down through it constantly, so keep the party out of one another's fall line and clear of the ropes. Do not attempt it in rock shoes. Plan on 2.5 to 3 hours in good conditions; parties benighted here describe about three hours of complex route-finding in the dark, and advise against starting it after dark.

text: Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. The way from camp is obvious once you're established there. The first-ascent party climbed from the notch south of the peak, reaching it from the west, then kept to the south and west sides of the mountain along obvious weaknesses — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on comparatively solid Pickets rock.

The original line gained the notch south of the peak, and gained it from the west rather than by attacking the notch directly from the glacier below, then stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses at easy-to-moderate fourth and low fifth class. text:
From the South Tieton Creek and Conrad Meadows trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, traverse onto the Meade Glacier, then finish over boulders, scree and a summit snowfield.

The Conrad is the more active of the peak's two small glaciers, so this line wants a rope, a harness and a crevasse-rescue kit rather than just an axe and crampons.

Descent reverses the traverse: back over the saddle and down the Conrad to Conrad Meadows. It is normally done over two or more days given the long approach through the drainage and the talus.

text:
Two glaciers with one saddle between them. That sequence is the route and it is the test.

You climb the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft, and from that saddle you traverse onto a second glacier — the Meade — before any of the summit ground. Glacier, saddle, glacier, then boulders, scree and a summit snowfield, in that order.

The negative at the saddle is the one worth carrying: if you reach a saddle and the ground beyond it is boulders and scree with no second glacier, you are on the wrong saddle. This route's saddle opens onto ice. A saddle that opens onto rock belongs to the ridge line, which is the peak's other route from the same trailhead.

The elevation is a cross-check rather than a marker: about 7,200 ft. Well above that and you have climbed the glacier past its col; well below and you are still on the apron.

Which side of the glacier matters and it is easy to get wrong in the dark: the east side of the Conrad. Drifting west takes you up the glacier's other flank and away from the saddle.

The approach-side finding: this route comes at the peak from the north. If you have climbed onto a long ridge with the peak in view along it, you are on the Klickton Divide line instead — a fine route, a different day, and it does not need a rope.
